s: The Objectives specified in the Preamble contain the basic structure of our Constitution. In this regard, choose the correct answer.
o: Basic structure means that which can be amended with a simple majority
Basic structure means that which cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368 of the Constitution

Basic structure refers to Fundamental Rights only
x: Basic structure means the features that cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Art. 368 (Kesavananda, 1973). It is not limited to the DPSPs or the FRs, and nothing in it is amendable by simple majority.

s: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that –
o: Certain features of the Constitution are so essential to
Fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away
The Constitution cannot be amended except in
The Preamble of the Constitution cannot be amended
x: The theory means certain features of the Constitution are so essential that they cannot be abrogated even by amendment. FRs can still be abridged, and the Preamble can be amended, subject to the basic structure.

s: The doctrine of 'the Basic structure of the Constitution' as a principle of Judicial Review
o: Accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts
Accepts the theory of supremacy of Legislature
Assumes the power of judging the Legislature
Is strictly in accord with the Principle of Procedure established by Law
x: By reviewing even constitutional amendments, the doctrine accepts the supremacy of the Constitution and of the courts (judicial supremacy 'to a limited extent'). It is not 'strictly in accord with procedure established by law' – under that principle a court only checks that the authority acted within its powers, so option D is wrong.

s:
Consider the following statements about the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution:

I. The doctrine of the 'Basic Structure' has been incorporated into the Constitution of India by an Act of Parliament.

II. Presently, the Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution of India can amend any part of the Constitution without affecting the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

III. Parliament's limited power to amend the Constitution is also an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

IV. The Supreme Court in the 'Kumar Padma Prasad Case' (1992) has declared that the mandate to build a 'welfare state' is an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: I is false (the doctrine is judge-made, not an Act). II is true (Parliament may amend any part without affecting the basic structure). III is true (limited amending power – Minerva Mills). IV is false: Kumar Padma Prasad (1992) concerned judicial independence; welfare state goes with Kesavananda/Bhim Singhji.

x: Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) advocated the absolute sovereign power of the monarch, since people surrender all rights to the sovereign. Locke favoured limited government and Rousseau popular sovereignty.

x: The Social Contract (1762) was written by Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Hobbes wrote Leviathan, Locke Two Treatises of Government.

x: D.G. Ritchie is an exponent of the historical (customary) theory of rights – rights grow out of custom. Locke stands for natural rights.

s: The state is a necessary evil according to
x: Individualists see the State as a necessary evil, to be kept minimal; anarchists want it abolished, so they are not the answer.

s: The concept of "National rights" was emphasised by
x: 'National rights' is a misprint for natural rights: John Locke made the natural rights of life, liberty and property the basis of government; Dalton, Leacock and Bryce did not.

s: Who among the following proposed the theory of 'Civil Legitimacy'?
x: Unkeyed: 'civil legitimacy' is not a standard theory name. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau all grounded the legitimacy of civil government in a social contract, and no source attributes the phrase to one of them, so no option can be fixed.

s: Which one of the following factors constitutes the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy?
x: Separation of powers, with checks and balances among legislature, executive and judiciary, is the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy. Centralisation endangers liberty; an elected government alone is not enough.

s: The Presidential Government operates on the Principle of
o: division of powers between Centre and States
x: The presidential system rests on separation of powers between executive and legislature; the parliamentary system rests on fusion. Division of powers between Centre and States is federalism.

s: Which organ of the government consists of elected representative of people?
x: The legislature (Parliament and State Legislatures) consists of the people's elected representatives. The media is not a government organ and judges are appointed.

s: In Indian Polity, the executive is subordinate to the-
x: In India the executive is subordinate to the legislature: the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)).

s: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution, the President of India enjoys the power to withhold his assent to any Bill passed by both the Houses of the Parliament?
x: Article 111 lets the President assent, withhold assent or return a non-Money Bill passed by both Houses; Art. 108 is the joint sitting, Art. 109 Money Bill procedure and Art. 63 the Vice-President.

s: In pocket veto, the President of India can keep a bill for how much duration?
x: In a pocket veto the President neither assents, rejects nor returns the Bill; Art. 111 prescribes no time limit, so he can hold it for an indefinite period.

s: Does the President of India have veto power?
o: The constitution is silent on this
x: Yes – the Indian President has the absolute, suspensive and pocket vetoes; he lacks only the qualified veto.

s: Identify the wrong statement with regard to Veto Power of the President of India.
o: He cannot return a Money Bill passed by the Parliament.
He has no Veto Power over Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368.
He has no Veto Power over an Ordinary Bill passed for second time by the Parliament.
He cannot Veto a Money Bill passed by the State Legislature duly forwarded by the Governor of a State.
x: (d) is wrong: for a State Money Bill reserved by the Governor, the President may assent or withhold assent, so he can veto it. The others are right – a Money Bill cannot be returned, an amendment Bill must be signed (24th Amendment) and a re-passed ordinary Bill must be assented to.
